source: Mattar & Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay
finding: Replay is a backup chosen by utility = gain x need. Gain is the policy improvement from the backup. Need is discounted expected future visits to that state. One rule yields both forward and reverse replay.
numbers: Simulations: beta=5, alpha=1.0, gamma=0.9; linear track 2 x 1x10 segments, 50 episodes; open field 6x9 grid, 50 episodes; 20 planning steps at episode start and end; significant replay = run of >=5 backups by permutation test. Paper gives no numeric simulation results, only qualitative.
quote: planning and learning are better understood as different variants of the same operation
limits: Model, not an experiment. Authors say gain needs the backup's effect on the policy known in advance, 'admittedly unrealistic'. Deterministic, stationary worlds; one-step myopic backups; replays only experienced transitions.
agent_relevance: Defines the ordering rule our memory operator could use: revisit the stored subgoal with highest (change it would cause) x (chance it is needed soon).

source: Mattar & Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay - reward and familiarity predictions
finding: Model predictions that separate it from a simple 'replay what was recent' rule: reverse replay rises with reward size and falls to near zero when reward is removed, while forward replay stays roughly flat; replay events drop with experience; replay starts at or behind the agent.
numbers: Cited data used for comparison: Diba & Buzsaki 2007 841/887 forward events before a run, 395/464 reverse after; Davidson 2009 n=136 cells 4 rats; Ambrose 2016 5 rats; Olafsdottir 2015 n=212 cells 4 rats; O'Neil 2008 613 cells over 33 novel sessions, 14 rats.
limits: Data are rodent place cells in simple mazes; match to the model is qualitative, no formal model comparison with rival rules.
agent_relevance: Gives testable signatures: reward change should raise reverse-style (credit) revisits, not forward-style (planning) ones.

source: Ambrose, Pfeiffer & Foster (2016) Reverse replay of hippocampal place cells is uniquely modulated by changing reward
finding: Reverse replay tracks reward change. Reward 4x at one track end raised reverse replay but not forward replay. Removing reward cut replay at that end.
numbers: N=5 rats; 7 sessions Exp 1, 8 Exp 2. Exp 1: 738 replays; reverse z=3.57 p=3.6e-4; forward z=0.305 p=0.76; forward vs reverse z=4.30 p=0.0001. Exp 2 (reward removed): 409 replays; reverse z=-2.05 p=0.041; forward z=-1.83 p=0.068 (n.s.); stopping 3.3 s vs 8.5 s. Only 15-20% of ripples held significant trajectory replay.
limits: Five rats. Under stricter criteria the authors saw zero reverse replays at the removed reward. Rats scan and sniff instead of eating, a behavioural confound. Reverse-replay drop on reward removal is only p=0.041.
agent_relevance: Core support for the gain half of the theory: new reward raises credit-style (backward) revisits. Effect is real but fragile on the negative side.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021) Hippocampal replay reflects specific past experiences rather than a plan for subsequent choice
finding: Replay content did not predict the next choice. It favoured previously rewarded places, especially the previous goal arm, and arms not visited recently. This partly fits gain/need but argues replay does not drive trial-by-trial planning.
numbers: 4 rats, 24/32/23/33 sessions. Search trials 711/848/725/1065; repeat trials 1347/1661/1154/1730. Current-goal replay rose with reward: R2=0.033/0.015/0.012/0.025. Previous-goal replay vs later visits: p=0.49/0.32/0.18/0.08 (no relation). Future-arm replay under once per trial. Correct-vs-error classifier near chance.
limits: Four trained rats, one task, correlational. Null results do not rule out indirect routes. Authors say replay 'seems unlikely to implement the value updates that could drive behavior'.
agent_relevance: Hard boundary: what gets revisited may reflect past reward and recency, not plans. Do not assume revisit order equals plan order in our scaffold; test it.

source: Liu, Mattar, Behrens, Daw & Dolan (2021) Experience replay is associated with efficient nonlocal learning
finding: First human test of utility. MEG replay at reward receipt was stronger for the high-utility (need x gain) non-local path, and reverse-direction replay went with better learning of non-local paths.
numbers: N=29. Backward replay (160 ms lag) high vs low utility t(28)=3.30 p=0.003; forward replay (30 ms) no difference p=0.74. Non-local learning rate 0.70 with 160 ms replay vs 0.61 without, p=0.023. Gain split: learning 0.79 vs 0.37 p=0.020. Need alone: 0.61 vs 0.54 p=0.16 (no effect). Need and gain uncorrelated r=-0.004.
limits: Correlational. Need-alone prioritisation not significant; the utility effect is an interaction. Lags chosen from the same data. Need took only 3 levels (17/33/50%). MEG source claims tentative.
agent_relevance: Best direct human support for gain x need, but need alone did not show. If we weight revisits, gain probably matters more than need.

source: Momennejad, Otto, Daw & Norman (2018) Offline replay supports planning in human reinforcement learning
finding: fMRI replay of earlier trajectories during rest predicted how much people changed plans after a reward change. No such link when reward was unchanged.
numbers: N=24 analysed of 26. Revaluation blocks Spearman rho=0.54 p=0.0068; control rho=-0.13 p=0.55; difference p=0.023. Replanning revaluation t(23)=4.89; control t(23)=-0.10. Replay fell Rest1 to Rest3 t(23)=2.9 p=0.007. Noise split only a trend p=0.066.
quote: offline replay of trajectories facilitates integrating representations that guide decisions
limits: Correlational. fMRI cannot see sub-second sequences. Only 4 blocks per person. Effect in noisy blocks just a trend. Signed vs unsigned prediction errors not separable.
agent_relevance: Replay is useful when something changed (gain) and idle when nothing changed. Supports triggering revisits on surprise, not on a schedule.

source: Liu, Dolan, Kurth-Nelson & Behrens (2019) Human replay spontaneously reorganizes experience
finding: Human replay at rest runs in sequences that follow learned abstract structure, not experienced order, and reverses direction after reward.
numbers: Study 1: 16/21 subjects forward sequenceness at 40 ms lag; 17/21 reverse after value learning. Study 2: forward replay of true sequence in 17/22. Reverse effect appeared in the first minute of rest (p=0.045).
limits: Two MEG studies of about 21-22 people each; reverse-after-reward shown as subject counts. Sequenceness methods are debated.
agent_relevance: Replay order can be reorganised by structure. A subgoal library should revisit in structural order, not log order.

source: Olafsdottir, Barry, Saleem, Hassabis & Spiers (2015) Hippocampal place cells construct reward related sequences through unexplored space
finding: Place-cell sequences pre-played a path to a seen but unvisited reward arm before the animal ran it. Replay is not limited to experienced transitions.
numbers: 4 rats, n=212 cells. Preplay events had higher ripple-band power than non-significant events. No bias to particular arm sections (cued p=0.22, uncued p=0.15).
limits: Contradicts the Mattar-Daw limit that replay only recombines experienced transitions. Preplay claims in general have contested null models.
agent_relevance: Revisit queue may need to include never-executed but seen options, not only past ones.

source: Carey, Tanaka & van der Meer (2019) Reward revaluation biases hippocampal replay content away from the preferred outcome
finding: Lead only, not opened (full text blocked). Title reports that after revaluation replay content favoured the non-preferred outcome, hard to fit with a pure gain-times-need account.
numbers: not recorded: paper not opened
limits: Not opened. Treat as an unverified lead; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Possible counter-example: revisit what is uncertain or avoided, not only what is best.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou & Silver (2016) Prioritized experience replay
finding: Machine-learning cousin of the idea: replay transitions with large TD error. Gives large speedups over uniform replay on Atari.
numbers: Better than uniform DQN on 41 of 49 games; median normalised score 48% to 106% (DQN); Double DQN median over 57 games 111% to 128%, mean 418% to 551%. Oracle ordering gives exponential speedup on Cliffwalk.
quote: picking the transitions in a good order can lead to exponential speed-ups
limits: TD error is a proxy for gain only; ignores need. Noisy transitions get over-sampled. Not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Ordering of memory access alone moves results a lot. Priority = size of surprise.

source: Hessel et al. (2018) Rainbow: combining improvements in deep RL
finding: Ablation: removing prioritised replay or multi-step learning hurt most games more than other components.
numbers: 57 Atari games; Rainbow median 223% (no-op starts), 153% (human starts); Prioritized DDQN 140% / 128%.
quote: The removal of either prioritization or multi-step learning reduces performance across most games
limits: Value varies per game; area-under-curve measure. Not about brain.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation at scale that ordering memory matters, tested by ablation.

source: Zhang & Sutton (2017) A deeper look at experience replay
finding: Boundary condition: a large replay buffer slows learning. Learning slowed as buffer grew from 100 to 1,000,000 in grid world, Lunar Lander and Pong. They propose combined experience replay (always add the latest transition) as an O(1) fix.
numbers: Default buffer 1e6 widely used; learning slowed as size rose from 1e2 to 1e6; Buffer-Q agents with very large buffers fail some tasks.
limits: Small tasks, simple function approximators. Does not test prioritisation directly.
agent_relevance: Large undifferentiated memory dilutes new information. Always include the latest item in the revisit set.

source: Fedus et al. (2020) Revisiting fundamentals of experience replay
finding: Bigger replay and fresher data help, but only with n-step returns. Other techniques, including prioritisation, gave limited benefit for sifting through larger memory.
numbers: Rainbow, capacity 1M to 10M; improvement tracks capacity and falls with age of oldest policy; removing n-step stops the gain. Only DQN+n-step improved with larger capacity among additive variants.
quote: these effects depend critically on the presence of a particular algorithmic component, n-step returns
limits: Atari, Dopamine Rainbow. Mechanism for n-step link not settled.
agent_relevance: Prioritising is not a cure for a big, stale memory. Freshness and multi-step credit matter as much.

source: Sujit, Nath, Braga & Kahou (2023) Prioritizing samples in RL with reducible loss (ReLo)
finding: Failed-replication-style result: PER (TD-error priority) hurt performance in several settings, e.g. SAC on Gym, and Seaquest and SpaceInvaders. Prioritising by learnability (steady loss drop) avoids it.
numbers: PER worse than uniform baseline in several settings; ReLo comparable or better; tested on DM Control, MinAtar, 24 Atari games (reduced steps), 5 seeds.
limits: Priority by learnability is itself a heuristic. Short Atari runs.
agent_relevance: High-surprise items can be noise. Gain must mean reducible error, not raw error.

source: Lahire, Geist & Rachelson (2022) Large batch experience replay (LaBER)
finding: Theory: the best sampling distribution is proportional to gradient norm. PER is a hyperparameter-sensitive heuristic. LaBER improves over base agents and other prioritisation schemes.
numbers: Tested on Atari, MinAtar and PyBullet; LaBER beats DQN with larger mini-batches. Per-game numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Per-game gains not recorded.
agent_relevance: Principled reading of priority: pick the memory that most reduces expected loss, i.e. gain.

source: Ma et al. (2026) Freshness-aware prioritized experience replay for LLM/VLM RL (FreshPER)
finding: Plain PER fails for LLM RL because stored priorities go stale as the policy changes. Multiplying priority by an exponential age decay fixes it.
numbers: 8 tasks, 0.5B/3B/7B models: +46% NQ Search, +367% Sokoban Simple, +133% VLM FrozenLake, +18% AIME vs on-policy; standard PER without decay consistently degrades. Decay constant 500 for Sokoban, 1000 for FrozenLake. Little benefit on GSM8K (>93% base) or CliffWalking.
limits: Preprint, one group. Gains of +367% start from a low base. Helps only when on-policy training struggles.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test. Stale priority is a real failure: our scaffold should decay stored gain estimates with age.

source: Sun et al. (2026) Difficulty-targeted online data selection and rollout replay for LLM RL
finding: Prefer moderate-difficulty questions and reuse recent rollouts. Cuts GRPO fine-tuning time while matching performance.
numbers: 6 LLM-dataset combinations; training time cut by 23% to 62% at the same performance as GRPO.
limits: Recent-only replay, not a gain x need rule. Saves time, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Moderate difficulty is a gain proxy: skip items already solved or hopeless.

source: Li et al. (2026) DyJR: dynamic Jensen-Shannon replay for RLVR
finding: Argues replay of accurate samples narrows the policy; keeps only temporally close samples (FIFO adaptive buffer) and a JS regulariser to keep diversity.
numbers: Abstract-level read only; numbers not extracted.
limits: Preprint. Numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Warning that replaying only successes reduces diversity; mix in alternatives.

source: Mattar & Daw (2018) stated limits and clinical speculation
finding: Authors list what is missing: no uncertainty, no process model for computing gain, one time scale, myopic single backups. They speculate faulty backup choice may relate to rumination.
numbers: See limits list in source.
limits: Speculation, untested.
agent_relevance: Gain is costly to compute exactly. An agent needs a cheap gain estimate, which the theory does not give.

source: Moore & Atkeson (1993) Prioritized sweeping
finding: Origin of priority-ordered backups in RL; cited by Schaul 2016 and Lahire 2022 as the root of PER. Not opened.
numbers: not recorded
limits: Not opened; claim taken from citing papers.
agent_relevance: Pedigree of the idea.

source: Diba & Buzsaki (2007) Forward and reverse hippocampal place-cell sequences during ripples
finding: Founding report: forward sequences before a run and reverse after. Numbers taken from Mattar & Daw's citation; original not opened.
numbers: 841 of 887 forward before run; 395 of 464 reverse after (as cited).
limits: Not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Origin of the forward-for-need, reverse-for-gain split.

source: Cross-source synthesis: where gain x need is supported
finding: Gain has support in human and rat data (Ambrose, Liu 2021, Momennejad). Need alone has weak support (Liu 2021 p=0.16). Replay-as-plan is contested (Gillespie 2021). Preplay of unexperienced paths (Olafsdottir 2015) breaks a model assumption.
numbers: Gain-linked effects significant in 3 of 3 studies tested (b03, b05, b06); need-only effect null in 1 of 1 (b05).
limits: Synthesis by this agent, not a meta-analysis. No formal meta-analysis of the theory was found.
agent_relevance: Weight revisits by expected change (gain) first; use need as a tie-breaker.

source: Cross-source synthesis: ML replay fails when priority is stale or noisy
finding: Three independent ML results show raw priority can hurt or add little: ReLo (b14, PER worse than uniform in several tasks), FreshPER (b16, plain PER degrades LLM RL), Fedus (b13, prioritisation limited benefit for larger memory).
numbers: See b13, b14, b16.
limits: Synthesis; settings differ (Atari, SAC, LLM RL).
agent_relevance: Design rule: priority = reducible gain x freshness; never raw surprise.

source: Search status note
finding: WebSearch quota was exhausted and arXiv search and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited. LLM-agent-memory papers using gain x need directly were not located. No LLM study found that tests Mattar-Daw utility by name.
numbers: none
limits: Gap: re-run when search budget returns.
agent_relevance: Open question for the team.

source: Liu et al. (2021) replay type and ripple link
finding: Two replay types dissociate: fast forward replay (30 ms lag) with ripple-band power and local path; slow backward replay (160 ms lag) with no ripple rise and non-local paths.
numbers: 30 ms replay ripple power t(28)=3.98 p=4.3e-4; 160 ms replay t(28)=0.64 p=0.53; difference p=0.0052. 160 ms replay strength vs reward per trial robust r=0.41 p=0.03; 30 ms r=-0.29 p=0.13.
limits: Many comparisons across lags and regions; across-subject link is one modest correlation.
agent_relevance: Planning-style and credit-style revisits may be separate processes; keep them as separate operators.
